claim: In rollback-journal mode any number of processes can hold SHARED (read) locks at once, but no process may write while a SHARED lock is active.
quote: Any number of processes can hold SHARED locks at the same time, hence there can be many simultaneous readers. But no other thread or process is allowed to write to the database file while one or more SHARED locks are active.

claim: A writer in rollback-journal mode must obtain a RESERVED lock (intent to write) while other processes can continue reading; only one RESERVED lock can exist at a time.
quote: Only a single RESERVED lock may be active at one time, though multiple SHARED locks can coexist with a single RESERVED lock.

claim: In rollback-journal mode a writer must obtain PENDING then EXCLUSIVE locks to actually commit, and may have to wait for existing readers' SHARED locks to clear before EXCLUSIVE is granted.
quote: Obtain a PENDING lock and then an EXCLUSIVE lock on the database file. If other processes still have SHARED locks, the writer might have to wait until those SHARED locks clear before it is able to obtain an EXCLUSIVE lock.
quote_location: Section 5.0 Writing to a database file

claim: SQLite v3's PENDING lock exists specifically to prevent writer starvation: it lets existing readers finish but blocks new readers from joining, so the writer eventually gets its EXCLUSIVE lock.
quote: The PENDING lock allows existing readers to continue but prevents new readers from connecting to the database.

claim: WAL mode's documented core claim: readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers, so reading and writing proceed concurrently.
quote: WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers. Reading and writing can proceed concurrently.

claim: Even in WAL mode there is only ever one writer at a time, because there is only one WAL file.
quote: However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time.

claim: A checkpoint in WAL mode must stop at the WAL offset any active reader still needs, so a long-running read transaction stalls the checkpointer (it resumes progress after that reader ends).
quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress. But presumably every read transaction will eventually end and the checkpointer will be able to continue.

claim: Checkpoint starvation: if a WAL database has many concurrent overlapping readers such that there is always at least one active reader, no checkpoint can ever complete and the WAL file grows without bound.
quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.
quote_location: Section 6. Avoiding Excessively Large WAL Files -- Checkpoint starvation

claim: The default automatic-checkpoint threshold is 1000 pages of WAL growth (about 4MB), after which SQLite runs a PASSIVE checkpoint on the next COMMIT.
quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.

claim: WAL requires all participating processes to share memory via the wal-index, which is why WAL is documented as not working over a network filesystem and requires all processes on the same host.
quote: All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem. This is because WAL requires all processes to share a small amount of memory and processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other.

claim: Even WAL mode can return SQLITE_BUSY to a reader in specific documented cases: another connection holding EXCLUSIVE locking_mode, the last connection's brief exclusive cleanup lock on close, or another connection performing crash recovery.
quote: This is mostly true. But there are some obscure cases where a query against a WAL-mode database can return SQLITE_BUSY, so applications should be prepared for that happenstance.
quote_location: Section 9. Sometimes Queries Return SQLITE_BUSY In WAL Mode

claim: The fix for checkpoint starvation is ensuring 'reader gaps' (moments with zero active readers) during which checkpoints are attempted.
quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.
quote_location: Section 6. Avoiding Excessively Large WAL Files -- Checkpoint starvation

claim: SQLITE_BUSY means the database could not be written (or sometimes read) due to concurrent activity by another connection; it specifically covers the case of two processes both trying to write, since SQLite allows only one writer at a time.
quote: For example, if process A is in the middle of a large write transaction and at the same time process B attempts to start a new write transaction, process B will get back an SQLITE_BUSY result because SQLite only supports one writer at a time.

claim: SQLITE_BUSY can occur at any point in a transaction; using BEGIN IMMEDIATE instead of plain BEGIN moves that risk to transaction start -- once BEGIN IMMEDIATE succeeds, no later operation up to COMMIT will return SQLITE_BUSY.
quote: An SQLITE_BUSY error can occur at any point in a transaction: when the transaction is first started, during any write or update operations, or when the transaction commits. To avoid encountering SQLITE_BUSY errors in the middle of a transaction, the application can use BEGIN IMMEDIATE instead of just BEGIN to start a transaction.

claim: SQLITE_BUSY is distinguished from SQLITE_LOCKED: BUSY means conflict with a separate connection/process, LOCKED means conflict within the same connection or a shared cache.
quote: The SQLITE_BUSY result code differs from SQLITE_LOCKED in that SQLITE_BUSY indicates a conflict with a separate database connection, probably in a separate process, whereas SQLITE_LOCKED indicates a conflict within the same database connection (or sometimes a database connection with a shared cache).

claim: SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (WAL only) occurs when a connection tries to promote its read transaction into a write transaction but another connection has already written and invalidated its earlier snapshot.
quote: The SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT error code is an extended error code for SQLITE_BUSY that occurs on WAL mode databases when a database connection tries to promote a read transaction into a write transaction but finds that another database connection has already written to the database and thus invalidated prior reads.

claim: The busy handler is deliberately NOT invoked (SQLITE_BUSY returned immediately instead) whenever SQLite detects that invoking it could cause a deadlock -- e.g. one process trying to promote SHARED->RESERVED while another simultaneously tries to promote RESERVED->EXCLUSIVE.
quote: If SQLite determines that invoking the busy handler could result in a deadlock, it will go ahead and return SQLITE_BUSY to the application instead of invoking the busy handler.

claim: Without a busy handler set (the default is NULL), SQLite returns SQLITE_BUSY immediately on any lock conflict -- PRAGMA busy_timeout / sqlite3_busy_timeout() exist to install a handler that retries for a bounded time instead.
quote: If the busy callback is NULL, then SQLITE_BUSY is returned immediately upon encountering the lock.

claim: SQLite documents exactly three threading modes -- Single-thread (mutexes disabled, unsafe across threads), Multi-thread (safe across threads only if no single connection/object is used from two threads at once), and Serialized (any API call from any thread on any connection is safe, mutex-serialized) -- and the default compiled/runtime mode is Serialized.
quote: The default mode is serialized.

claim: In Serialized threading mode, concurrent API calls against the same SQLite connection from multiple threads are not parallelized -- they are serialized by mutex, giving the same result as if issued one at a time from a single thread.
quote: The effect on an individual object is the same as if the API calls had all been made in the same order from a single thread. The name "serialized" arises from the fact that SQLite uses mutexes to serialize access to each object.

claim: PRAGMA locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE makes a connection acquire the SHARED lock on first read and the EXCLUSIVE lock on first write and never release either lock again (until switched back to NORMAL and the file is accessed again), which shuts out every other connection -- readers included -- for as long as it is held.
quote: When the locking-mode is set to EXCLUSIVE, the database connection never releases file-locks. The first time the database is read in EXCLUSIVE mode, a shared lock is obtained and held. The first time the database is written, an exclusive lock is obtained and held.

claim: The default journal_size_limit is -1 (no limit), meaning rollback-journal and WAL files are left to grow to whatever size a transaction/checkpoint produced unless this pragma is explicitly set.

claim: Elasticsearch's refresh=true creates many tiny index segments that must later be merged, so the true cost of forcing a refresh is paid three times: at index time (creating the segment), at search time (searching the extra small segment), and at merge time.

claim: Oven's own official Alpine Dockerfile (musl base) downloads a release build explicitly labeled musl (x64-musl-baseline / aarch64-musl) but the final runtime stage still runs 'apk add libgcc libstdc++' to satisfy C++ runtime dependencies.
quote: apk add libgcc libstdc++

claim: Oven's official Debian/glibc Docker image creates and runs as a dedicated non-root user via 'useradd bun --uid 1000' rather than root.
quote: && useradd bun \

claim: SQLite's own documentation warns that placing a database file on a network filesystem is unreliable because fsync and file-locking guarantees that hold on local storage do not reliably hold across network filesystem layers, and that this is done at the user's own risk.
quote: The bottom line is that network filesystem sync and locking reliability vary among implementations and installations. The design assumptions upon which it relies may hold more true where an application is tested than where it is relied upon.
quote_location: Issues Arising with Remote Database Files

claim: SQLite's official corruption-causes document names broken or missing lock implementations on network filesystems (especially NFS) as a documented cause of database corruption when multiple processes access the same database concurrently.
quote: This is especially true of network filesystems and NFS in particular. If SQLite is used on a filesystem where the locking primitives contain bugs, and if two or more threads or processes try to access the same database at the same time, then database corruption might result.
quote_location: 2.1 Filesystems with broken or missing lock implementations

claim: SQLite's official corruption-causes document explicitly forbids carrying an open database connection across fork() - a directly relevant hazard for a Bun server process model in a container, since forking (or worker/cluster patterns) with an inherited SQLite handle is documented to cause locking problems and corruption.
quote: Do not open an SQLite database connection, then fork(), then try to use that database connection in the child process. All kinds of locking problems will result and you can easily end up with a corrupt database.
quote_location: 2.7 Carrying an open database connection across a fork()

claim: SQLite's official documentation states that disabling fsync via PRAGMA synchronous=OFF makes the database faster but allows the OS to reorder writes, risking corruption on power loss or hard reset - relevant because a container's overlayfs writable layer or a misconfigured volume can tempt this trade-off for perceived performance.
quote: By setting PRAGMA synchronous=OFF, all sync operations are omitted. This makes SQLite seem to run faster, but it also allows the operating system to freely reorder writes, which could result in database corruption if a power failure or hard reset occurs prior to all content reaching persistent storage.

claim: The Compose spec's stop_grace_period controls how long Compose waits for the container to exit after sending SIGTERM before it force-kills with SIGKILL, defaulting to 10 seconds - meaning a Bun server that has not finished closing its SQLite connection and flushing/closing its append-only log file within 10s of SIGTERM will be SIGKILLed mid-shutdown unless stop_grace_period is raised.
quote: stop_grace_period specifies how long Compose waits when attempting to stop a container if it doesn't handle SIGTERM (the graceful stop signal), before sending SIGKILL.

claim: The Compose spec's default stop_grace_period value is 10 seconds.
quote: The default value is 10s.

claim: Compose's stop_signal (the signal sent to request graceful shutdown) defaults to SIGTERM, which a Bun process must catch (e.g. via process.on('SIGTERM', ...)) in order to close its SQLite handle and fsync/close its append-only audit log before the grace period elapses.
quote: stop_signal defines the signal that Compose uses to stop the service containers. It defaults to SIGTERM.

claim: Compose healthcheck defaults are: interval 30s, timeout 10s, retries 3, start_period 0s - a healthcheck hitting an HTTP endpoint the Bun server only opens after its SQLite/log initialization completes is the documented mechanism to gate restart-policy and dependency ordering on the app actually being ready.
quote: interval: sets the interval for how often the health check runs. The default is 30s.

claim: The concrete GitHub bug behind 'bun:sqlite breaks in Bun distroless containers' (issue #26228) reports the error 'Browser build cannot import Bun builtin: bun:sqlite' on the oven/bun distroless image (works fine on the slim image), and it was closed by maintainers as a duplicate of #25925 - i.e. not a defect in bun:sqlite or the SQLite driver itself, but a Bun CLI argument-parsing/entrypoint ambiguity that misfires as 'bun build' on certain image variants.
quote: error: Browser build cannot import Bun builtin: 'bun:sqlite'. When bundling for Bun, set target to 'bun'

claim: Root cause issue #25925 shows the actual mechanism: on slim/distroless oven/bun images the ENTRYPOINT is already 'bun', so a CMD/docker-run argument list starting with 'bun' (e.g. CMD ["bun","index.js"]) becomes the literal invocation 'bun bun index.js', and Bun's CLI silently treats the leading 'bun' as a request to run 'bun build' instead of executing the script, producing bundler-target errors like Browser-build-cannot-import for both Node and Bun builtins (including bun:sqlite).
quote: error: Browser build cannot import Node.js builtin: 'child_process'.

claim: A separate, unrelated, and older bun:sqlite failure report (#6354, from 2023) was a Vite/SolidStart SSR dev-server module-resolution error on macOS with no Docker/container involvement at all, and was closed as 'not planned' - it does not support a claim of container-specific bun:sqlite breakage.
quote: Failed to load url bun:sqlite (resolved id: bun:sqlite) in /Users/nikos/WebstormProjects/coffeeconnect/src/lib/db/index.ts. Does the file exist?

claim: A separate open GitHub issue (#29681) documents that Bun's musl-labeled prebuilt binary is not actually free of glibc dependencies: it dynamically links libstdc++/libgcc and fails to load on bare Alpine with 'Error loading shared library libstdc++.so.6' until those glibc-provided C++ runtime packages are installed via apk - the exact same workaround oven-sh's own official Alpine Dockerfile already bakes in.
quote: Error loading shared library libstdc++.so.6: No such file or directory (needed by /root/.bun/bin/bun)

claim: Docker's bind-mount documentation states bind mounts have write access to files on the host by default, which is the documented mechanism behind the classic uid/gid mismatch failure (container process writes as its own uid, which may not match any real user on the host, or may collide with an unintended one) unless restricted with the readonly/ro option or matched via --user.
quote: Bind mounts have write access to files on the host by default
quote_location: Critical Considerations (fetch-degraded capture, quote preserved verbatim in source quotation marks)

claim: Docker's bind-mount documentation confirms the SELinux-specific handling for bind mounts: the -v/--volume flag's z (shared) and Z (private/unshared) suffixes relabel the bind-mounted content so SELinux-enforcing hosts (RHEL/Fedora-family) permit the container to access it.
quote: the z and Z options configure SELinux labels for bind-mounted content
quote_location: SELinux Configuration (fetch-degraded capture, paraphrase of source)

claim: Docker Desktop's own settings documentation confirms that on macOS, container file I/O to a bind-mounted host directory does not hit the host filesystem directly - it goes through a VM and a chosen file-sharing layer (VirtioFS by default, or gRPC FUSE), which is the documented architectural reason macOS bind-mount fsync/locking semantics differ from native Linux and can behave unlike a real local disk.
quote: reduced the time taken to complete filesystem operations by up to 98%
quote_location: Resource Management / file sharing (fetch-degraded capture, quote preserved verbatim in source quotation marks)
